key_finding: Across six deep search agents on BrowseComp-Plus and BrowseComp, answer accuracy correlates strongly with cumulative retrieval recall but only weakly with number of search steps or context consumed, and the best-performing agents issue far fewer redundant queries.
methodology: Trajectory-level diagnosis of long-horizon search agents using human-annotated document-level relevance judgments, comparing six agents on BrowseComp-Plus and validating on BrowseComp with an open-web search API, retrieval model and harness held fixed.
why_it_matters: Shows that agentic search's presumed lever -- more searching -- often fails to deliver, redirecting attention from search volume to query formulation, evidence selection, and stopping criteria; directly informs how to attribute agentic gains and where they stop holding.
limitations: Six agents on two related benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp); may not generalize to literature-search-specific benchmarks
Diagnostic/correlational analysis rather than a causal ablation of each mechanism
relevance_reason: Directly diagnoses which agentic search behaviors carry the gain and which are low-yield, bearing on decisions 2 and 4.

key_finding: PaSa-7B exceeds the best Google-based baseline by 37.78% in recall@20 and 39.90% in recall@50 on RealScholarQuery, and outperforms a prompted GPT-4o agent (PaSa-GPT-4o) by 30.36% in recall and 4.25% in precision.
methodology: RL-trained LLM agent that issues search queries, reads papers, and selects references, trained on a synthetic 35k-query dataset (AutoScholarQuery) and evaluated on a human-curated real-world benchmark (RealScholarQuery).
why_it_matters: Provides both a benchmark-construction template (synthetic RL training set plus a real-world eval set) and a strong quantified anchor for how much an agentic reference-following/reading loop can gain over single-query search-API baselines like Google.
limitations: Trained on synthetic data that may not transfer to all query types
Baselines (Google, ChatGPT) are uncontrolled live search, unlike fixed-corpus benchmarks
relevance_reason: A leading exemplar agentic paper-search system with quantified gains over search-API baselines and its own benchmark construction, central to decisions 1-3.

key_finding: Crase, which does one seed search then a bounded 1.5-hop citation-graph expansion with entailment-based pruning and recency-aware ranking, outperforms deep research agents built on proprietary models by up to 3x recall@50 at roughly a third of the cost on LitSearch and a further benchmark over a 500K-paper arXiv corpus.
methodology: Bounded and inspectable pipeline: one search-engine query for seed papers, 1.5-hop citation neighborhood expansion, entailment-based edge pruning, recency-aware random-walk ranking; evaluated on LitSearch and one further benchmark over a 500K-paper arXiv corpus.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates that a fixed, inspectable citation-graph-traversal design beats open-ended deep-research agent loops at much lower cost, directly answering which specific agentic move (bounded graph traversal with pruning) should be built rather than an unconstrained search loop.
limitations: Evaluated on only two benchmarks (LitSearch and one further)
Compares against 'deep research agents' as undifferentiated systems rather than isolating which of their components underperform
relevance_reason: A concrete, bounded citation-graph-traversal design with quantified recall/cost comparisons, directly answering decision 2.

key_finding: Overlap between human- and AI-selected references was under 6% across eight expert research projects; 64% of mid-2025 LLM-generated references had at least one incorrect metadata field, though a 2026 model showed zero fabrication or mismatch in a single-project test.
methodology: Controlled study of eight expert-conceived literature-review tasks in physics/astrophysics/cosmology comparing human-expert and LLM (ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT Deep Research, Gemini) reference selections and auditing reference accuracy for fabrications and metadata mismatches.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the premise that current agentic literature-search systems reproduce expert-quality search: reference overlap with experts is minimal and hallucination/metadata-error rates were high in mid-2025 models, recalibrating how much trust reported agentic gains deserve without independent verification.
limitations: Small sample: eight projects in one broad domain area
Improved-model result is a single-project test, not systematically validated
relevance_reason: Empirically shows agentic literature-search assistance fails to replicate expert-level search quality, directly serving decision 4.

key_finding: WisPaper's agentic Deep Search module achieves 22.26% recall on TaxoBench versus 20.92% for an O3 baseline, with its validation submodule (WisModel) reaching 93.70% accuracy at mitigating retrieval hallucinations.
methodology: End-to-end agent system combining keyword retrieval with an agentic 'Deep Search' validator using structured reasoning; evaluated on TaxoBench. Abstract-only for further detail.
why_it_matters: The reported agentic gain over a strong non-database LLM baseline (O3) is small (about 1.3 recall points), an example that tempers how much credit agentic validation modules deserve versus simpler baselines.
limitations: Gain over baseline is marginal and reported on a single benchmark (TaxoBench)
No ablation isolating which module (keyword search vs Deep Search validator) drives the gain
relevance_reason: An agentic literature-search system whose reported gain over an LLM baseline is thin, relevant to how much agentic mechanisms actually add.

key_finding: ReBOL, seeding a Bayesian-optimization posterior over relevance with LLM query reformulations and iteratively acquiring document batches for LLM scoring, achieves 46.5% vs 35.0% recall@100 against the best LLM reranker baseline on Robust04, with comparable NDCG@10 and latency.
methodology: Multimodal Bayesian Optimization over document relevance initialized by LLM query reformulations and refined via iterative LLM query-document scoring, evaluated against LLM-reranker baselines on five BEIR datasets with two LLMs.
why_it_matters: A concrete retrieval/reranking technique combining query reformulation with iterative relevance optimization that could underlie the retrieval layer of an agentic literature-search system, though tested on general BEIR IR benchmarks rather than a scientific-literature-search setting.
limitations: Evaluated on general BEIR retrieval datasets, not a scientific-literature-search benchmark
No evaluation of the technique inside a full agentic literature-search pipeline
relevance_reason: A retrieval/reranking method combining query reformulation and iterative relevance optimization, matching C3 but outside the brief's literature-search setting.

key_finding: Removing followable cross-reference links from a generated wiki-style corpus roughly doubles search cost per grounded fact at scale, though grounded coverage stayed at ceiling in all conditions and previously 'unreachable' facts were recovered via read-derived re-search when links were absent.
methodology: Pre-registered two-arm contrast planting a deterministic generated corpus (50/500/5000 pages) with real hyperlinks vs. meaning-preserving prose links, evaluated with a Claude agent across 99 episodes on an MCP-based wiki search/fetch tool.
why_it_matters: Offers a loosely analogous controlled test of how removing graph/link structure affects an LLM agent's search cost, but the setting is a synthetic organizational wiki rather than scientific-literature citation graphs, limiting direct transfer.
limitations: Domain is a synthetic organizational wiki, not scientific-literature citation graphs
Single agent (Claude) and deterministic synthetic corpus limit generalizability
relevance_reason: Studies how removing link/graph structure affects agentic search cost, a weak analogy to citation-graph traversal but in an off-domain setting.

key_finding: LATTICE, an LLM-guided hierarchical search index with calibrated path-aggregated traversal, matches the best fine-tuned ensemble baseline at 46.7 nDCG@10 on BRIGHT with a single off-the-shelf LLM, and an ensemble variant (LATTICE++) reaches 49.1 nDCG@10.
methodology: Top-down LLM-guided construction of a hierarchically navigable search index from multi-level document summaries, plus calibrated LLM-guided traversal with cross-branch reference nodes; evaluated on BRIGHT, NQ, SciFact, SciDocs.
why_it_matters: Quantifies where embedding-retriever-plus-LLM-verifier pipelines fail on reasoning-intensive queries (the recall-ceiling problem) and offers an alternative retrieval architecture removing the embedding model from the search-time loop, directly bearing on decisions 1 and 3.
limitations: Primary benchmark (BRIGHT) is reasoning-intensive IR rather than literature-search-specific
Advantage over reranking only appears after a moderate token budget
relevance_reason: A retrieval/reranking method that measures where single-query embedding retrieval fails, directly addressing decisions 1 and 3.

key_finding: On the fixed-corpus BrowseComp-Plus benchmark, Search-R1 with BM25 achieves only 3.86% accuracy versus GPT-5's 55.9%, and pairing GPT-5 with a Qwen3-Embedding-8B retriever raises accuracy to 70.1% with fewer search calls.
methodology: A benchmark derived from BrowseComp using a fixed, curated corpus with human-verified supporting documents and mined hard negatives, enabling controlled, disentangled comparison of deep-research agents and retrievers.
why_it_matters: Gives a controlled, corpus-fixed measurement of the gap between a weak baseline retriever (BM25) and a strong agentic+embedding combination, directly anchoring the size of the agentic gain over single-query search and enabling disentangled retriever-vs-agent analysis.
limitations: Corpus (~100K docs) assembled per-query from the benchmark's own supporting docs and mined negatives, which later work shows may inflate measured performance
Single benchmark domain (BrowseComp-style web queries), not literature-search specific
relevance_reason: The central controlled benchmark for measuring baseline retrieval vs agentic deep-research gains, foundational to decisions 1 and 4.

key_finding: NIS-Agent, applying context isolation at webpage-triage and final-answer-validation to counter a newly identified 'inertia bias' where agents judge their own prior actions less objectively, reduces token cost by 33% while maintaining competitive performance on GAIA, WebWalkerQA, BrowseComp, and BrowseComp-zh.
methodology: Introduces the IBIS benchmark controlling search observations while varying self-authorship of prior actions to isolate inertia bias; proposes NIS-Agent and evaluates it across four deep-research benchmarks, plus an 8B model trained for intrinsic resistance.
why_it_matters: Identifies a specific, previously unattributed agent failure mode and a targeted fix, refining what should be measured and built beyond generic 'more search,' relevant to isolating which agentic component actually drives gains.
limitations: IBIS benchmark's construction details are not given in the abstract
Improvement framed mainly as cost reduction/competitive parity rather than large accuracy gains
relevance_reason: Attributes a measured improvement to a specific mechanism (context isolation against inertia bias), relevant to decision 2 and to where reported gains come from.

key_finding: HySemRAG's structured-extraction pipeline achieves 35.1% higher semantic similarity (0.655 vs 0.485, p<0.000001) than PDF-chunking RAG, with 68.3% single-pass QA success and 99.0% citation accuracy across 643 evaluation observations.
methodology: Eight-stage ETL+RAG pipeline combining semantic search, keyword filtering, and knowledge-graph traversal with agentic self-correction and post-hoc citation verification; evaluated on 643 observations over 60 testing sessions, applied to geospatial epidemiology literature.
why_it_matters: A working hybrid retrieval-plus-agentic-correction system for literature synthesis, useful as a comparison point for retrieval design, though its reported gains are attributed to the pipeline as a whole rather than isolated to a specific agentic move.
limitations: Gains reported for the system as a whole with no ablation isolating which hybrid component or the self-correction step drives the improvement
Validated primarily on one applied domain (geospatial epidemiology)
relevance_reason: A hybrid retrieval and agentic-correction literature-synthesis system relevant to C3, but weak on isolating the agentic mechanism (C2).

key_finding: A systematic taxonomy of Deep Research agent architectures (static/dynamic workflows, single/multi-agent) accompanies a critical review finding current benchmarks limited by restricted external-knowledge access, sequential-execution inefficiencies, and misalignment between evaluation metrics and DR agents' practical objectives.
methodology: Narrative survey and taxonomy of information-acquisition strategies (API vs browser-based), tool-use frameworks, and agent architectures, with critical benchmark evaluation. Abstract-only for review methodology.
why_it_matters: Synthesizes the field's benchmarks and architectures and flags specific evaluation misalignments, giving a map of what has and hasn't been validated and where benchmark critique should focus for decisions 3 and 4.
limitations: Narrative review without a stated systematic protocol
Descriptive taxonomy rather than new empirical evidence on baseline-vs-agentic gains
relevance_reason: The field's own review of deep-research-agent design and benchmark limitations, a synthesis point against which other shortlisted findings can be checked.

key_finding: Relocating BrowseComp-Plus's evidence into the independently-built ClimbMix corpus (yielding 57 fully-grounded questions) drops the strongest agent's evidence recall from 84.3% to 21.4% and increases search calls by 63%, while answer accuracy falls only five points.
methodology: A projection pipeline decomposes benchmark questions into atomic reasoning hops and re-grounds each hop in a new 553M-document corpus (ClimbMix) built without reference to the benchmark, verifying every hop via automatic checks, an independent agent, and human review.
why_it_matters: Shows that a widely-used deep-research benchmark's reported retrieval performance depends heavily on its query-selected corpus construction and largely evaporates once decoupled from that construction -- the clearest evidence here that reported agentic gains are partly a benchmark-construction artifact.
limitations: Only 57 of 830 original questions survive full grounding verification, a small resulting set
Single benchmark (BrowseComp-Plus) projected onto a single alternative corpus (ClimbMix)
relevance_reason: Directly demonstrates a reported agentic/retrieval gain shrinking dramatically under a construction-decoupled benchmark, the strongest evidence for decision 4.

key_finding: PaperPilot-9B, trained via workflow imitation and preference optimization over an executable DAG of search operators, raises Hit@5 from 58.0 to 77.0, MRR from 47.5 to 59.4, and nDCG@10 from 26.8 to 32.5 over the base toolset agent while cutting workflow execution errors from 9.5% to 0%.
methodology: Supervised workflow imitation plus preference optimization over controlled workflow corruptions; multi-turn evaluation against a Qwen3.5-9B toolset-agent baseline.
why_it_matters: Decomposes literature-search agent behavior into named operators (keyword search, citation expansion, reranking, evidence extraction) with per-operator gains, giving direct evidence on which agentic moves carry improvement rather than treating the system as a black box.
limitations: compares against an in-house toolset-agent baseline rather than a plain single-query search baseline
benchmark construction for the eval set is not described
relevance_reason: Directly evaluates a multi-operator agentic literature-search system and attributes gains to specific search-workflow components, core to decision 2.

key_finding: Separating residual-query reformulation from graph evidence aggregation improves multi-hop retrieval by up to 5.59 Recall@5 points and 4.50 F1 points over the strongest baseline on 2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue.
methodology: Graph retrieval architecture combining original and residual (evidence-derived) query signals, propagated across entity-linked propositions; evaluated on three multi-hop QA benchmarks.
why_it_matters: A clean demonstration that query reformulation driven by already-retrieved evidence, not the original query alone, is what carries gains in graph-structured retrieval — a mechanism directly relevant to how citation-graph traversal should be designed in literature-search agents.
limitations: evaluated on general multi-hop QA benchmarks, not scientific literature search
no comparison to single-query database search baseline
relevance_reason: Isolates the specific contribution of evidence-guided query reformulation in graph retrieval, informative for C2/C3 even though the setting is QA rather than literature search.

key_finding: Coding 26 AI-scientist systems across seven audit dimensions finds 83% release code but only 38% release execution traces and 38% report any novelty-verification method, with no system demonstrating an externally validated in-loop oracle.
methodology: Systematic screening of 125 candidate works, full-text coding of 26, across lifecycle stage, autonomy level, evaluation method, and verification artifacts.
why_it_matters: Warns that reported capability claims for agentic research systems, including literature-search components, are largely unverified by external checks, which should temper how much weight the scan gives to self-reported gains anywhere in this literature.
limitations: covers the full AI-scientist lifecycle rather than literature search specifically
abstract gives no per-stage (e.g. literature-search) breakdown of the verification gap
relevance_reason: A survey of verification practices across agentic science systems; touches the brief's skepticism about unreplicated gains but is not focused on literature-search benchmarks.

key_finding: PaSaMaster achieves 16.5x higher F1 than Google Scholar and 37.8% higher F1 than GPT-5.2 at about 1% of the cost across 38 disciplines, while reducing source hallucination from 32.66% to zero.
methodology: Recursive self-evolving retrieval combining frontier-LLM intent understanding with lightweight-model retrieval/scoring over verified papers; evaluated on PaSaMaster-Bench (38 disciplines).
why_it_matters: Directly anchors the single-query search baseline (Google Scholar) the brief asks for and quantifies the size of an agentic gain against it, giving a concrete number to check other reported improvements against.
limitations: benchmark (PaSaMaster-Bench) construction methodology not detailed in the abstract
gain not decomposed into the contribution of individual agentic moves
relevance_reason: Provides an explicit single-query database search baseline (Google Scholar) and a large measured gain over it, central to decision 1.

key_finding: PaperQA2 matches or exceeds subject-matter-expert performance on retrieval, summarization, and contradiction-detection tasks, and identifies 2.34±1.99 contradictions per paper with 70% expert validation.
methodology: Human-AI comparison study on real-world literature research tasks; introduces the LitQA2 benchmark that guided PaperQA2's design.
why_it_matters: The widely-cited paper establishing the premise this scan is asked to interrogate — that agentic literature-search systems beat expert human search — so every later claim of gain or failure-to-replicate should be read against it.
limitations: comparison is against human experts, not a single-query database search baseline
no decomposition of which agentic components drive the reported performance
relevance_reason: Foundational, highly-cited claim of superhuman literature-search performance that the rest of the field argues with or tries to replicate.

key_finding: Across custom and provider-native agent harnesses, grep-based retrieval generally outperforms vector retrieval on a 116-question LongMemEval sample, with overall accuracy depending strongly on harness and tool-calling style even given identical underlying data.
methodology: Two controlled experiments comparing grep vs. vector retrieval across multiple agent harnesses (Chronos, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI), with inline vs. file-based tool outputs and varying distractor volume.
why_it_matters: Directly undercuts the assumption that embedding/vector retrieval is the stronger baseline agentic systems should build on — a finding that should make the scan question whether reported agentic gains over dense-retrieval baselines are measuring the retrieval method or the harness.
limitations: evaluated on conversational memory (LongMemEval), not scientific literature search
does not test citation-graph traversal or query reformulation directly
relevance_reason: Empirically shows a simple lexical baseline beating vector retrieval depending on harness design, relevant to the brief's baseline-ceiling and replication questions even outside the literature-search domain.

key_finding: GraphRAG-Bench shows GraphRAG frequently underperforms vanilla RAG on real-world tasks, and systematically characterizes the conditions (task type, pipeline stage) under which graph structure actually helps.
methodology: New benchmark spanning fact retrieval, complex reasoning, contextual summarization, and creative generation, with end-to-end pipeline evaluation from graph construction through generation.
why_it_matters: Directly tests the premise underlying citation-graph traversal in agentic literature search: the graph mechanism itself does not reliably beat plain retrieval, and this benchmark's task-by-task breakdown is the template for checking whether a literature-search agent's graph traversal is actually earning its keep.
limitations: built on general-domain RAG tasks rather than scientific literature corpora
graph retrieval technique (GraphRAG) is generic; findings are inferred to transfer to citation-graph traversal rather than tested on it directly
relevance_reason: The clearest existing evidence that a graph-based retrieval mechanism's reported gains can shrink or vanish depending on task and benchmark, which is exactly the failure mode decision 4 asks the scan to find, and the underlying GraphRAG technique is the same one used in literature-search citation traversal.

key_finding: DynaKRAG's learned, state-conditioned policy for coordinating iterative retrieval, query reformulation, and sufficiency checking ranks first on EM/F1 across all nine dataset-backbone pairs while cutting total tokens by 10.1-34.3% and retrieval calls by 15.1-43.4%.
methodology: Unified evidence-action framework with a validity layer, continuation gate, and advantage scorer; evaluated on HotpotQA, 2Wiki, and MuSiQue across three LLM backbones against matched-backbone baselines.
why_it_matters: Shows that explicit, learned coordination of iterative retrieval and query reformulation operations (rather than an undifferentiated agent loop) yields consistent efficiency and quality gains — evidence for which specific agentic moves are worth building, even though it's demonstrated on QA rather than literature search.
limitations: evaluated on multi-hop QA benchmarks, not scientific literature retrieval
baseline is a matched-backbone method, not a single-query database search
relevance_reason: A close methodological analogue for decision 2 — decomposing iterative-retrieval/query-reformulation gains — but off the brief's literature-search setting.

key_finding: Deep research agents evaluated on six public benchmarks show widespread Search-Time Contamination — retrieval of benchmark metadata, question context, or answers via web search — inflating measured performance by up to 4%.
methodology: Defines three contamination severities (metadata, question-context, explicit-answer leakage) and develops detection algorithms applied across six public benchmarks and modern deep research agents.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete, measured mechanism by which reported agentic gains are inflated rather than real, and a corresponding remediation (isolated sandboxes, contamination-aware evaluation) that should shape how any benchmark used in this scan's decision 3/4 is trusted.
limitations: deep research agents studied do general web research, not scientific-literature-specific benchmarks
4% inflation figure is aggregate across six benchmarks, not broken out per benchmark type
relevance_reason: Directly answers decision 4 — showing exactly how and how much reported agentic search gains can be an artifact of benchmark contamination rather than a real capability gain.

key_finding: Deep Research Bench's 89 human-scored multi-step web research tasks show that offline 'RetroSearch' agents (frozen scraped web pages) perform comparably to live-web agents, enabling stable evaluation of research agents over time.
methodology: 89 task instances across 8 categories with human-worked-out answers; frozen web-snapshot RetroSearch environment; automated trace evaluation for hallucination, tool use, and forgetting across released LLMs.
why_it_matters: A model for how to build a contamination-resistant, reproducible benchmark for agentic search systems — directly informative for decision 3 on how evaluation sets for literature-search agents should be constructed to avoid the moving-target problem.
limitations: tasks are general web research, not scientific literature search specifically
no single-query database search baseline reported
relevance_reason: A methodological template for benchmark construction (frozen corpus, human-labeled multi-step tasks) transferable to literature-search agent evaluation, though built for general web research.

key_finding: The MTEB-leading embedding retriever (59.0 nDCG@10) scores only 18.3 nDCG@10 on BRIGHT's reasoning-intensive queries, though incorporating explicit reasoning about the query recovers up to 12.2 points.
methodology: 1,384 real-world, curated queries spanning economics, psychology, mathematics, and coding, requiring reasoning beyond surface-form matching; extensive evaluation of state-of-the-art retrievers.
why_it_matters: The sharpest available quantification of how far single-query embedding search's recall ceiling falls on reasoning-heavy queries — exactly the kind of number decision 1 needs, even though the domains tested are not scientific literature.
limitations: queries drawn from general reasoning domains, not scientific literature search
does not evaluate agentic, multi-turn, or graph-traversal retrieval systems directly
relevance_reason: Foundational retrieval benchmark demonstrating a large, quantified single-query recall ceiling gap that anchors decision 1, widely used as a stress test in this literature.

key_finding: Agents-K1 converts 2.46 million scientific papers into an agent-native knowledge graph (Scholar-KG, one-million-paper subset released) via a multimodal parser, a 4B GRPO-trained extraction backbone, and a tri-source CLI unifying web search, graph retrieval, and cross-document traversal, improving scientific information extraction, KG construction, and multi-hop reasoning.
methodology: Multimodal document parsing into typed entities/claims/evidence/relations, reinforcement-learned information extraction, and an agent interface unifying web search with multimodal graph retrieval and citation traversal; evaluated on constructed knowledge graphs at scale.
why_it_matters: A concrete design for citation-graph traversal beyond flat 'cites' edges — capturing entities, claims, and method lineages — directly bearing on what the graph-traversal component of an agentic literature-search system should represent.
limitations: no comparison against a single-query database search baseline
benchmark/evaluation construction beyond 'extensive experiments' is not detailed in the abstract
relevance_reason: Proposes a richer citation-graph representation and traversal interface specifically for scientific literature agents, directly actionable for the system-design question in decision 2.

key_finding: An agent that dynamically selects between GraphRAG (Neo4j citation KG) and VectorRAG (FAISS + hybrid reranking) per query, with instruction-tuned DPO generation, gains 0.63 in Context Recall and 0.56 in Context Precision over baseline on synthetic literature-review queries.
methodology: Pipeline ingesting PubMed/arXiv/Google Scholar metadata into a Neo4j citation graph and FAISS vector store (all-MiniLM-L6-v2), with a Llama-3.3-70B agent choosing GraphRAG vs. VectorRAG per query and DPO-tuned generation, bootstrapped evaluation on synthetic benchmarks.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates a concrete architecture that decides per-query whether graph traversal or vector search is worth invoking, giving an empirical answer to which agentic move (graph vs. vector) to route to, directly usable for system design.
limitations: evaluated on synthetic benchmarks mimicking real queries rather than a validated literature-search benchmark
gains reported per metric are modest and not decomposed by query type
relevance_reason: A directly on-topic agentic hybrid-RAG system for scientific literature review that attributes gains to a specific dynamic graph/vector routing mechanism, central to decision 2.

key_finding: A keyword-based (sparse) retrieval and distillation system for scientific literature review achieves results close to state of the art on biology QA benchmarks without needing dense retrieval infrastructure.
methodology: LLM-based search-and-distill system evaluated against biology-related questions from prior literature benchmarks; compares sparse vs. dense retrieval approaches.
why_it_matters: Suggests the retrieval-quality gap the brief assumes agentic/dense methods must close may be smaller than believed, which changes how much credit later gains should give to retrieval sophistication versus distillation.
limitations: biology-domain only
compares against prior benchmarks rather than constructing a new evaluation set
no explicit ablation isolating which agentic move drives coverage gains
relevance_reason: Directly tests whether simple sparse retrieval approaches the recall ceiling claimed for more complex agentic literature-search systems.

key_finding: Search-based LLM agents' benchmark scores are partly inflated because retrieval surfaces the evaluation dataset itself (e.g., on HuggingFace) for ~3% of questions, and blocking that source drops accuracy on the contaminated subset by ~15%.
methodology: Empirical audit of agent search logs on HLE, SimpleQA, and GPQA, including an ablation after blocking HuggingFace as a retrievable source; logs publicly released.
why_it_matters: Directly answers Q4: shows a documented mechanism by which reported agentic-search gains are artifacts of benchmark leakage rather than genuine reasoning, meaning any gain must be checked for search-time contamination before being trusted.
limitations: studied on general-knowledge benchmarks (HLE, SimpleQA, GPQA) rather than scientific-literature-search benchmarks specifically
identifies only one contamination channel (HuggingFace) though notes others may exist
relevance_reason: Provides concrete evidence of a benchmark-construction flaw that inflates agentic search gains, exactly the failure mode the brief wants surfaced.

key_finding: Integrating sparse and dense retrieval signals within a contextual citation-graph structure (CG-RAG/LeSeGR) significantly outperforms RAG methods using state-of-the-art retrieval approaches on research question-answering benchmarks.
methodology: Introduces a contextual graph representation for citation graphs and a hybrid lexical-semantic graph retrieval method, evaluated against multiple retrieval baselines across domains.
why_it_matters: Isolates citation-graph traversal combined with hybrid retrieval as the specific mechanism carrying the gain, directly answering which agentic move (Q2) and which retrieval technique (C3) matters.
limitations: benchmark construction details for the research-QA evaluation are not elaborated
no discussion of whether gains hold under a different benchmark or replication
relevance_reason: A close match to the system-design question: attributes measured gains specifically to citation-graph traversal plus hybrid retrieval, not to an undifferentiated agent.

key_finding: State-of-the-art LLMs achieve only 0.40 accuracy with no retrieval on FRAMES multi-hop questions, rising to 0.66 with a multi-step retrieval pipeline (>50% relative improvement).
methodology: Introduces FRAMES, a unified factuality/retrieval/reasoning benchmark of challenging multi-hop questions, with baseline and multi-step retrieval pipeline results.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete no-retrieval vs. multi-step-retrieval baseline gap that is useful for calibrating how much of a reported agentic gain is retrieval-driven versus reasoning-driven.
limitations: general multi-hop factual QA rather than scientific-literature search specifically
does not isolate which agentic move (reformulation, graph traversal, crawling) drives the multi-step gain
relevance_reason: Offers a well-constructed benchmark and baseline numbers relevant to Q1/Q4, but its setting is general QA rather than scientific literature search.

key_finding: On 130 long-horizon agentic web-search tasks (Mind2Web 2), the best system (OpenAI Deep Research) reaches only 50-70% of human performance despite using half the time, evaluated via a novel Agent-as-a-Judge rubric framework.
methodology: New benchmark of 130 realistic long-horizon tasks built with over 1000 hours of human labor; introduces tree-structured rubric Agent-as-a-Judge for automatic correctness/attribution scoring; evaluates ten frontier systems plus humans.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates a rigorous approach to constructing and judging agentic search benchmarks with long horizons, directly informing how the project should measure gains beyond static single-query baselines.
limitations: general web browsing/deep-research tasks, not scientific-literature search specifically
no explicit attribution of gains to individual agentic mechanisms
relevance_reason: High-quality benchmark-construction and evaluation methodology for agentic search systems, in a closely neighboring setting to scientific literature search.

key_finding: ReMindRAG uses LLM-guided knowledge-graph traversal with memory replay (storing traversal experience in edge embeddings) to improve both effectiveness and cost efficiency over existing KG-RAG baselines.
methodology: Train-free method combining node exploration, node exploitation, and memory replay over knowledge-graph edges; evaluated across multiple benchmark datasets and LLM backbones.
why_it_matters: Provides a concrete, measurable graph-traversal mechanism (memory replay) that could underlie citation-graph traversal in literature-search agents, informing which specific traversal design choices carry gains.
limitations: evaluated on general knowledge graphs, not citation graphs of scientific literature
no benchmark construction details or contamination controls discussed
relevance_reason: Graph-traversal mechanism directly analogous to citation-graph traversal, though tested outside the scientific-literature setting.

key_finding: A three-agent (Query, Retrieval, Learning) system combining BM25 sparse and FAISS dense retrieval achieves an 8.5% precision and 7.3% recall improvement plus ~210ms lower latency versus PaperQA and Semantic Scholar.
methodology: FastAPI-based multi-agent architecture with hybrid BM25/FAISS retrieval and Sentence-Transformer semantic matching, benchmarked against published retrieval systems.
why_it_matters: Directly attributes measured precision/recall gains to a specific agentic component (the Query Agent's expansion/refinement), giving concrete evidence for Q2 in the exact scientific-literature-search setting.
limitations: published outside a peer-reviewed venue (venue not listed)
no description of evaluation set construction or contamination controls
small reported citation count suggests limited independent verification
relevance_reason: A directly on-topic multi-agent scientific literature search system with quantified baseline comparisons and mechanism attribution.

key_finding: InfoDeepSeek introduces a benchmark for agentic information seeking in dynamic web environments, built via a systematic methodology ensuring query determinacy, difficulty, and diversity, revealing nuanced agent behaviors across LLMs and search engines.
methodology: New benchmark and evaluation framework with fine-grained accuracy/utility/compactness metrics, tested across multiple LLMs, search engines, and question types.
why_it_matters: Gives an explicit, criteria-based methodology for constructing challenging agentic-search evaluation sets, directly informing how the project should judge whether a literature-search benchmark's construction is sound (Q3).
limitations: general web information-seeking rather than scientific-literature search specifically
no explicit contamination controls comparable to search-time contamination studies
relevance_reason: Strong benchmark-construction methodology for agentic search evaluation, in a neighboring but not identical setting to scientific literature search.

key_finding: OpenNovelty, an LLM-agentic system that extracts contribution claims, retrieves prior work via semantic search, and performs full-text comparisons, was deployed on 500+ ICLR 2026 submissions and preliminary analysis suggests it surfaces closely related prior work authors may overlook.
methodology: Four-phase pipeline (query generation, retrieval, taxonomy construction, synthesis) grounded in retrieved real papers; deployed at scale with reports published, but evaluation is preliminary/qualitative.
why_it_matters: A live example of an agentic literature-retrieval system built for a real scholarly task, illustrating query-generation-plus-retrieval design choices, though it offers no quantitative gain attribution or baseline comparison.
limitations: preliminary analysis only, no rigorous quantitative evaluation
no comparison against a single-query database search baseline
no benchmark construction or contamination discussion
relevance_reason: A directly on-topic agentic scientific-literature-retrieval system, but with weak evidentiary support for any specific decision.

key_finding: A systematic survey decomposes the 'deep research' agent pipeline into four stages (planning, question developing, web exploration, report generation), categorizing representative methods, optimization techniques, and benchmarks for each.
methodology: Narrative/systematic survey of autonomous research agent literature; abstract-only for specifics beyond the four-stage taxonomy.
why_it_matters: Provides the field's own organizing taxonomy of which agentic moves (query development, web exploration) are distinguished from the system as a whole, directly shaping how the scan should categorize and sequence Q2 and Q3 evidence.
limitations: abstract-only, no quantitative results given
narrative overview rather than a systematic-protocol review
covers deep research broadly, not scientific literature search exclusively
relevance_reason: The synthesis paper most directly organizing the space the brief asks about, useful for structuring the rest of the scan's findings.

key_finding: ReasonIR-8B, trained on synthetic reasoning-focused query/hard-negative data, achieves 29.9 nDCG@10 (36.9 with reranker) on the BRIGHT reasoning-retrieval benchmark and improves RAG performance on MMLU (+6.4%) and GPQA (+22.6%).
methodology: Synthetic data generation pipeline producing challenging queries and hard negatives per document; retriever trained on a mixture of synthetic and public data; evaluated on BRIGHT and downstream RAG tasks.
why_it_matters: A state-of-the-art reasoning-intensive retriever that could underlie the dense-retrieval component of agentic literature-search systems, relevant to C3, though not evaluated in a scientific-literature-search setting.
limitations: evaluated on general reasoning-retrieval benchmarks (BRIGHT, MMLU, GPQA), not scientific-literature search specifically
no discussion of citation graphs, iterative crawling, or benchmark construction for literature search
relevance_reason: A strong underlying retrieval method potentially usable in agentic literature-search pipelines, but tested outside the brief's target setting.

key_finding: OpenScholar-8B, retrieving from 45 million open-access papers, outperforms GPT-4o by 5% and PaperQA2 by 7% in correctness on the newly built ScholarQABench (2,967 expert queries, 208 long-form answers across four domains), while GPT-4o hallucinates citations 78-90% of the time versus OpenScholar's expert-level citation accuracy.
methodology: Retrieval-augmented LM with self-feedback inference loop, evaluated on a purpose-built multi-domain literature-search benchmark against strong closed and open baselines, plus human preference evaluation.
why_it_matters: Directly establishes both a benchmark-construction template (C4) and a baseline/gain comparison (C1/C3) for scientific-literature-search systems, the exact setting the brief targets.
limitations: comparisons rely on specific baseline systems (GPT-4o, PaperQA2) that may not represent all single-query search baselines
does not test whether gains hold under a different benchmark or independent replication
relevance_reason: A foundational system-and-benchmark pair squarely in the brief's target setting, informing both design and evaluation decisions.

key_finding: On LitSearch's 597 realistic literature-search queries, there is a 24.8% absolute recall@5 gap between BM25 and state-of-the-art dense retrievers, LLM-based reranking further improves the best dense retriever by 4.4%, and commercial search engines lag the best dense retriever by 32 points.
methodology: Benchmark of 597 queries constructed from GPT-4-generated questions on cited paragraphs plus author-written questions about recent papers, expert-reviewed; extensively benchmarks retrieval models and two LLM reranking pipelines.
why_it_matters: Directly supplies the single-query BM25 baseline recall ceiling (Q1) the brief asks for, plus a rigorously constructed evaluation set (Q3) and a measured reranking gain (C3), making it a reference point every later agentic-gain claim should be checked against.
limitations: benchmark centers on recent ML/NLP papers, so generalization to other scientific fields is untested
does not evaluate full agentic pipelines (reformulation, graph traversal, iterative crawling), only retrieval and reranking
relevance_reason: The clearest, most directly on-topic baseline-and-benchmark paper for scientific literature search retrieval.

key_finding: Introduces DeepResearch Bench, a 100-task PhD-level benchmark across 22 fields with two novel evaluation methodologies — a reference-based report-quality metric and a citation-accuracy/effective-citation-count framework — both shown to align strongly with human judgment.
methodology: Benchmark construction paper: 100 expert-crafted research tasks across 22 domains, paired with a reference-based adaptive-criteria scoring method and a separate citation-count/accuracy evaluation framework for information retrieval capability; open-sourced.
why_it_matters: Directly answers the benchmark-construction question the brief prioritizes: it specifies how tasks were sourced (domain-expert crafted), what is labeled (reference-based adaptive criteria), and how retrieval/citation quality is separately scored — a template against which other agentic-search benchmarks' construction choices (and any contamination or labeling shortcuts) should be compared.
limitations: abstract does not report a single-query/database-search baseline for comparison, so the recall ceiling question is untouched
no discussion of whether agentic gains replicate across benchmarks or metrics
focused on general deep-research/web-exploration agents rather than scientific-literature-search agents specifically, though closely adjacent
relevance_reason: A widely-cited (214 citations) benchmark paper whose dual evaluation methodology for report quality and citation accuracy is exactly the kind of benchmark-construction evidence the brief's third decision needs.
